Wheat-Marketing of Surplus

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We intend to be competitive. We think we have some control over the competitive situation. The North American supplies are the largest in the world and I do not think we in North America need panic if one country in another part of the world decides to cut its price below ours. It is almost inevitable that we in North America will hold some kind of blanket over the smaller exporting countries.
How do you intend to do it? Will you do as you did in 1935? Will you throw it on the market?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What market?
The world market.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We did not do
that.
Your party did.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: But prices were very much better after we took over. I will give you the figures, if you like. I have all sorts of figures here.
Do not screen the figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: When my hon. friend from eastern Canada starts dreaming about prices we get some funny results.
The figures are not so important as the principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, I will give the figures. You asked for them.
No, I asked for the principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend begins to take interest when? I suppose about the thirties. Does he?
I was interested a long time before that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We will start with 1927. That was a good year. These are farm prices: in 1927-28-and these are bureau of statistics figures-the price was 98 cents per bushel on the farm; 1928-29 it was 78 cents a bushel on the farm; in 1929-30 it was $1.03 on the farm; in 1930-31-I guess this must have been after the election-it was 47 cents a bushel on the farm; in 1931-32 it was 37 cents on the farm; in 1932-33 it was 34 cents on the farm-that was a great year and that figure was the average price on the farm for wheat; in 1933-34 it was 47 cents on the farm; in 1934-35 it was 60 cents on the farm; and then, what was the year we had the fire sale?-1935-36; the average price for 1935-36 was 60 cents; in 1936-37 it was 92 cents and in 1937-38 it was $1.03.
That is the year you sold it to the farmer when there was a crop failure. You sold it to them for seed.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Well, one would think that the prices must have got better when the government changed.
We have had several solutions offered for this problem. I think perhaps the most fantastic one is that by the hon. member for Assiniboia who deals in fantastic ideas. We are members of the international wheat agreement and we are partners with, I think, 48 other countries in that agreement, but in spite of that the hon. member suggests we have several other agreements. First, he would have an agreement with the United States to sell at the same price.
Co-operate.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Co-operation, yes, but it must be an agreement and no nonsense about it. Then next he suggests an agreement with the United Kingdom and that would be a special agreement under which we would supply wheat to the United Kingdom and, I suppose, as an inducement we could give them a lower price. Is that it? I think that after you had made these three agreements you would be a little confused as to who was agreeing with whom. But in any case it is a fantastic idea and I shall not pursue it.
You were pretty proud about the United Kingdom agreement when you had it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: But now we have other agreements.
As long as your government signed it you were proud of it, but when someone else suggests it then the idea is fantastic.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: All right, but one agreement at a time. Three at one time are too many. Then we have the old perennial that we should sell our wheat for sterling. That is a very good idea except that I do not know of anyone who wants to buy our wheat for sterling. The United States has been proposing the sale of wheat in local currency and I know only of two sales which have been put through on that basis. One was to Japan and the provision in that case was part gift and part sale. The part sale was conducted in yen which was to be used for the support of the United States army in that country. The other was a sale to Spain and part of that sale is to be paid for in pesetas and the pesetas are to be used in constructing aeroplane bases in that country.

Is there one with West
Germany?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, they sell 1 or dollars to West Germany. Germany is practically a hard currency country today. Any country can apply to the United States for the purchase of wheat and for payment in the local currency, but they do not seem to do that. The reason is that a debt in local currency is just as difficult for most countries as a dollar debt and people prefer to trade in the currency of the country where the purchase is made.
Now, there is another fallacy, namely, that there are millions of starving people in this world who would be glad to get the wheat if someone gave it to them. I wish people who make that statement would just tell me where those people are and how we can get wheat to them. Pakistan had a bad time and the United States and Canada helped them. We gave a certain amount of wheat to Pakistan against Colombo plan funds. The United States I think gave a very big quantity of wheat. What happened? Pakistan was just not able to take all the wheat that the United States offered them and has not taken it to this day. Why? Because they could not put it into consumption.
Everybody suggests that India is a country that would be delighted to take gifts of wheat. India happened to have very good crops last year. The monsoons came at the right time. They have not been purchasers of wheat except to a very small extent and then mostly for milling and reshipment. They are not needing wheat as a gift from anybody and would not take it if it was offered.
Those are the areas most often spoken about as being the possible recipients for great quantities of wheat to feed starving people. I do not know of any. If my hon. friend knows of a place, I think we would consider very carefully helping out starving people wherever we find them; but I do not know where they are. I wish my hon. friend and other hon. members of this house who keep referring to the fact that there are starving peoples who would be glad to take large quantities of surplus wheat if we were willing to give it away would just remember these facts.
After all, the wheat trade of the world is one of the most ancient trades of all. Wheat has been moving between countries for, I suppose, a thousand years or more. Certain practices in the trade have developed, and those practices are just as good today as they were at any other time. Most countries prefer to deal in wheat as they have always dealt in it, namely, to buy it where they can buy it most cheaply on the basis of quality and
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus to pay for it in the currency of the country that supplies the wheat. Until I hear of many more sales in local currencies or of many more countries asking for the gift of wheat, I shall continue to believe that the methods of disposing of wheat being followed by the Canadian wheat board are those that are acceptable to our customers in all parts of the world.
As will have been noted from the figures I quoted for world consumption, world consumption is substantially down this year. Why? Because almost every country in the world had a bumper crop of wheat. Countries that have never exported previously have become exporters of wheat this year. Sweden has been a substantial exporter of wheat, as was Turkey. France has been exporting considerable quantities of wheat. France has been exporting more wheat than usual, although France in some years is an exporter and in other years is an importer. It is a country that is almost in balance of production against consumption.
We have had an unusual year and, of course, we on this continent harvested our third greatest crop. It is a problem we have to deal with. It has been said that the producers in the west are having an extremely tough time because they cannot deliver their wheat. May I point out that they are delivering the normal quantity of wheat, or more than the average of the past ten years.
Their production is almost twice as large.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I know their production is great; and if they could market it all they would have twice as much money as they have now. All I am pointing out is that they are marketing the normal quantity of wheat and they are receiving the normal income averaged over the last ten years.
Is it not true that at the present time the figures are about 170 million bushels short of what they were last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I know. Last year was an extraordinary year. I have read the figures. It was the greatest marketing year that this country has ever seen. We never before sold nearly as much grain in a year as we sold last year. I wish the world consumption of wheat every year would permit us to sell that quantity of grain as our share of world markets. Unfortunately the number of bushels that make up our share of the world market depends on the over-all size of the world market. This year the total amount of wheat entering world markets is much smaller than it was last year.
As I say, we had representatives of western Canada in Ottawa at the agriculture

Wheat-Marketing of Surplus committee. I took that opportunity to have a talk with each of them in order to find out whether, in his opinion, there was a need for supplementary income in western Canada. Some of them had taken a poll among their locals and were able to give me the result of the poll. The results of the polls that were taken showed that a small percentage-I think it was 1 per cent in the case of Saskatchewan-reported a need for supplementary financing.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question at that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Was not the discussion based upon a loan with an interest rate of 5 per cent or 6 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We were discussing a loan; yes.
The farmers already have more debt than they can handle; they do not want any more.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: A farmer who worries about interest rates is not short of necessities, at any rate. A man in dire need does not worry about interest rates.
He may not be starving when his granaries are full of wheat, but he is short of everything else.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext: And the farmer takes the rap.
Make your own speech.
You helped me make mine so I am helping you make yours.
You needed help.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
What is the difference
between driving ahead and R. B. Bennett's blasting?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We do not blast; we just hold what we have. We try very hard to do that. We have customers among the countries of the world. We know about the proportion of Canadian wheat that those countries are accustomed to take. We watch them closely. If they are not buying from us when our turn comes, we make inquiries to find out why. If it is a matter of price, that is one factor which, added to other factors, may indicate to the wheat board that a cut in price is necessary.
Those are the facts of life. That is the policy that the wheat board will follow. It is the purpose of the board to be competitive. Anyone who has tried to hold wheat off the market for a period in this country has headed for disaster. If proof of that statement is needed, I might refer back to the period from 1930 to 1935, which started with the holding of wheat off the world market.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the minister referred back to 1930 to 1935, I should like to refer back to a little bit more recent date when he insisted on $2.05 a bushel for wheat with regard to the United Kingdom market. From what the minister has just now said, surely we are to take it that this new policy is an abrupt change, a right-about-face, from the time when you held out for $2.05 with the United Kingdom. According to the statement you have just made tonight, you are going to sell wheat even if you have to cut the price further, and you are going to meet world competition and sell wheat wherever you can sell it, even though you have to reduce the price again.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad my hon. friend brought that up because I intended to touch on that- another fallacy. My hon. friend likes to bring up the fallacies and it gives me a chance to straighten out his ideas regarding the situation. When the delegates from the 42 importing countries and the 4 exporting countries met in Washington to revise the wheat agreement Canada was represented as an exporter. The purpose of the meeting, among other things, was to determine maximum and minimum prices for a new agreement. The United States took a very extreme view. I believe they started by asking for a maximum price of $2.50. The importing countries asked for a maximum price of $1.80.
Canada believed that both these were extreme and our efforts were largely devoted towards bringing the United States down to

a more reasonable view of a maximum price as well as attempting to bring the importing countries up to a more realistic price. After a great deal of negotiation 41 of the 42 importing countries agreed to accept $2.05. It was not Canada's price. It was a compromise between all the exporters and all the importers with Canada lending her best offices to bring about a meeting of the minds. After that meeting of minds was arrived at the United Kingdom announced that it was not prepared to sign the agreement. That country said that it would not go beyond $2.00. All the other 41 importing countries agreed to the maximum price of $2.05. Consequently at that stage the only question was whether Britain would or would not sign the agreement setting a price of $2.05 and Britain decided not to sign.
However, I point out that that was the maximum price. There was also a minimum price fixed, the minimum price being $1.55. The assumption is that if we have maximum and minimum prices there is an area between the two which is a trading area, and that is where the price of wheat is today. It is below the maximum and above the minimum, about half way between the two at the present time, and under conditions of surplus supplies in the exporting countries it is my opinion that it is a reasonable area within which the present price should be established.
My hon. friends can talk about maximum prices as though that meant something more than the term implies. It is true that there was pressure from the importing companies which kept the price at the maximum for a number of years. That pressure does not exist today. The pressure, if any, is from the exporting countries which are seeking to reduce their surpluses. But the average price of Canadian wheat today is $1.75i. In other words, it is about half way between the maximum and minimum prices. The price at Fort William is $1.72J and the price at Vancouver is $1.78i, and about half the grain is going to the west coast and half to the east coast. The price of $1.75 is not a bad split between $1.55 and $2.05. That is the price today. There is room for movement in either direction. A bad crop in one of the exporting countries, even in Canada, would probably move the price up, and another bumper crop would very likely move it down. But we have that area between $1.55 and $2.05 for trading before either the maximum or the minimum prices of the international wheat agreement become effective. I think that I have now explained government policy and exposed the fallacy of the ideas put forward by the opposition, and I will resume my seat.

Mr. Speaker, the speech just delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) outside of its historical review, in parts inaccurate and in other parts incorrect, leaves little hope for the Canadian farmer in the position in which he is today. I cannot understand why the minister did not tell the house and the country something of what has taken place between Canada and the United States with reference to this matter. There have been several meetings apparently designed to prevent or at least to postpone a price war among the wheat-producing nations of the world. There was a meeting in March between the cabinet ministers of Canada and the United States. What took place there? With the exception of a slight amount of information that the government has deigned to give to the house, there remains a blackout as far as Canadians are concerned.
Only yesterday the Australian minister for commerce and agriculture forecast a situation that should have been dealt with this evening by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He said that the slashing of prices is apt to continue and he goes on to point out that there could easily be a repetition of the depression story when a similar price war forced wheat below two shillings. What Canadians would have liked from the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not the rather jovial speech he delivered this evening, not as replete as usual with optimistic prophecy but nonetheless made in a jovial way; they would have liked him to give them hope, but what he pointed out may well happen. Further reductions may take place in order to meet world competition.
That can lead only to a very serious position for agriculture. What Canada would have liked to hear from the minister tonight is something of what the Canadian government has done with respect to pointing out to the government of the United States the terrible danger to the nations today of any policy in the nature of price cutting at this time which inevitably will cause difficulty and stress and create a dangerous situation in agriculture within our country.

Can we get any information? Yesterday I tried to ascertain what happened last week when there was a meeting in Washington between Canadian and United States representatives. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said he was not there and apparently did not know. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he was not there. If there ever was a conference where nobody was there and yet much apparently was decided it was that of ten days ago in Washington.
What Canadians are asking for today, what the western farmer is asking for today-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Everybody should eat more wheat.

-is something in the nature of a declaration by Canada with respect to the efforts it is making in reference to the United States to prevent anything in the nature of price cutting competition in wheat sales. But all we receive from the minister is a historical review of the thirties. Let me say this about the thirties. The Conservative party inherited exactly the same condition as prevails today as the result of world conditions, and a condition that arose while the Liberal party was in power. It is no use reliving that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You will not inherit this one, John.

What Canadians want to know is what is the government going to do? What is its policy? What we received tonight was a historical review that gave no hope and little future to the western farmer who has asked parliament today to let him know what ti e situation is.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Prince Albert moves that this debate do now adjourn. Before we adjourn I want to make a few observations at this time so that hon. members will consider them and perhaps give me their own views at a later stage. The amendment reads:
This house is of the opinion that in view of the present grave situation in the matter of international wheat trading the government should make an immediate declaration as to its policy respecting the marketing of our Canadian wheat surplus.
Now is it an amendment to ask that the government make an immediate declaration of its policy? An amendment has a certain objective, and the objective is to alter the main question so as to help hon. members state their position on policies. Is it an amendment, even if the amendment to a


motion to go into supply has not to be relevant, to ask that the government make an immediate statement of policy? Is it a parliamentary motion? That is the first question I should like to submit to hon. members.
The second question is this. I was away for a while looking over these amendments, and upon my return to the chair was informed that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had made a speech. When he spoke a moment ago, what did he do? Even if that declaration of policy by the minister was not to the liking of hon. members, is it not a fact the minister has expressed the policy of the government because he is the spokesman with respect to these various matters, and according to the theory of cabinet solidarity he has spoken for the government. Has he not complied with the terms of this amendment? That is another point I should like to submit to hon. members for their serious consideration.
Of course when one considers that the amendment asks for a declaration of policy from the government, one could go a little further. After all the government, by the constitution, are the advisers of Her Majesty. They are the ones who are supposed to propose policy. Can we, by an amendment or by a decision of this house, force the government to declare their policy if they do not wish to do so? I have in my hand here a treatise on parliament by C. Ilbert who was a Clerk of the House of Commons in England and the author of several books. On page 111 of this particular book he says, under the title "administration":
Parliament does not govern. Parliamentary government does not mean government by parliament. Once, and once only, in the course of English history has the House of Commons attempted to administer the affairs of the country through executive committees, and the precedent by the long parliament has not been followed.
What is done by parliament, and especially by the House of Commons, is in the first place to secure that the King's ministers, who control and are responsible for the executive government of the country, shall represent and have the confidence of the party, or combination of parties, which commands a majority in the house, and in the next place to control the action of those ministers by means of questions and criticisms.
Now, is this a criticism? The amendment asks that the government declare a policy immediately. I submit these observations for the benefit of hon. members. Of course if the amendment is not in order, then the subamendment is not in order either.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As a subamendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Well, at the moment that is what we are considering. It is a subamendment. Considering that now the original question must be laid aside for the time

being, the amendment so to speak becomes a distinctive motion. The amendment to the amendment spells out a policy. The amendment was to the effect that the government should state its policy immediately. I consider that the policy has already been stated. Then the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) in his subamendment spells out what the policy should be. He says:
. . . that the government should give consideration to including in such policy the provision of a floor price to the wheat producers of Canada at levels not less than the Canadian wheat board selling price, basis Fort William-Port Arthur on Friday, June 4, 1954.
Aside from other considerations if this amendment were in order, and if it were carried by the house, would it not have the effect of giving a direct order to make a public expenditure? On this point I refer hon. members to previous rulings which I ask them to consider. There is the ruling of Mr. Speaker Black on May 24, 1932, page 515 of the Journals; another by Mr. Speaker Glen on March 29,	1943, page 213 of
Wheat-Marketing of Surplus the Journals; another one by the same Speaker on March 30, 1943, page 221.
As I said a moment ago, I am not making a ruling at this moment but I am asking hon. members to seriously consider the observations I have made. When we resume the discussion of these amendments, we can hear the views of hon. members. If I am wrong in my contention, I can take into consideration the remarks that might be made by experienced hon. members of the house, and I would be very pleased to revise what I would otherwise consider to be perhaps a quite sound ruling.
